Negative Binomial-Generalized Exponential Distribution

Source: R/nbge.R
NBGE.Rd

Density, distribution function, quantile function, and random generation for the negative binomial-generalized exponential (NBGE) mixture: a negative binomial (NB2) count whose mean is multiplied by a generalized exponential random effect with mean one.

Usage

dnbge(x, mu, shape, alpha, log = FALSE)

pnbge(q, mu, shape, alpha, lower.tail = TRUE, log.p = FALSE)

qnbge(p, mu, shape, alpha, lower.tail = TRUE, log.p = FALSE)

rnbge(n, mu, shape, alpha)

Arguments

x

vector of (non-negative integer) quantiles.

mu

vector of (positive) means.

shape

vector of (positive) shape parameters \(k\) of the generalized exponential mixing distribution.

alpha

vector of (non-negative) NB2 dispersion parameters; alpha = 0 gives the Poisson-generalized exponential distribution (dpge).

log, log.p

logical; if TRUE, probabilities p are given as log(p).

q

vector of quantiles.

lower.tail

logical; if TRUE (default), probabilities are \(P(Y \leq y)\), otherwise \(P(Y > y)\).

p

vector of probabilities.

n

number of observations. If length(n) > 1, the length is taken to be the number required.

Value

dnbge gives the probability mass, pnbge the distribution function, qnbge the quantile function, and rnbge random deviates. The length of the result is determined by n for rnbge, and is the maximum of the lengths of the numerical arguments for the other functions.

Details

The distribution is defined hierarchically: $$X \sim \mathrm{GE}(k, 1), \quad F_X(x) = (1 - e^{-x})^k, \quad G = X / A, \quad A = \psi(k + 1) - \psi(1),$$ $$Y \mid G \sim \mathrm{NB2}(\mathrm{mean} = \mu G, \mathrm{dispersion} = \alpha),$$ where \(\psi\) is the digamma function, so that \(E[G] = 1\) and the conditional variance is \(\mu G + \alpha (\mu G)^2\). With \(B = \psi'(1) - \psi'(k + 1)\) and \(M_2 = 1 + B / A^2\) (\(= E[G^2]\)), $$E[Y] = \mu, \qquad \mathrm{Var}[Y] = \mu + \left((1 + \alpha) M_2 - 1\right)\mu^2.$$ The scale of the generalized exponential distribution cancels in this mean parameterization and is not a parameter. \(\alpha = 0\) gives the Poisson-generalized exponential distribution and, as the generalized-exponential heterogeneity vanishes, the distribution approaches NB2. The two dispersion mechanisms have confounded effects on the variance, so \(k\) and \(\alpha\) are only separately identified through the shape of the distribution; expect weak identification in small samples.

This construction is specified here; a distribution with a similar name elsewhere may be defined differently.

Probabilities are computed on the log scale by adaptive quadrature over the logarithm of the mixing variable (the same deterministic, mode-centred rule as dpge), so tail probabilities keep their relative accuracy. Upper tails are summed directly from the probabilities. Random deviates are generated from the definition.

References

Gupta, R. D. and Kundu, D. (1999). Generalized exponential distributions. Australian & New Zealand Journal of Statistics, 41(2), 173-188.

Greene, W. (2008). Functional forms for the negative binomial model for count data. Economics Letters, 99(3), 585-590.

Examples

dnbge(0:6, mu = 2, shape = 1.5, alpha = 0.5)
#> [1] 0.36375462 0.22612339 0.13793589 0.08665409 0.05615242 0.03739404 0.02549160
# alpha = 0 gives the Poisson-generalized exponential distribution
all.equal(dnbge(0:10, mu = 2, shape = 1.5, alpha = 0),
          dpge(0:10, mean = 2, shape = 1.5, scale = 1))
#> [1] TRUE
pnbge(5, mu = 2, shape = 1.5, alpha = 0.5)
#> [1] 0.9080144
qnbge(c(0.5, 0.95), mu = 2, shape = 1.5, alpha = 0.5)
#> [1] 1 7
set.seed(8)
y <- rnbge(5000, mu = 2, shape = 1.5, alpha = 0.5)
c(mean = mean(y), var = var(y))
#>    mean     var 
#> 2.08040 9.06975
